analysis.one_liner: Lets states pool existing federal health money to run their own universal health coverage programs.
analysis.headline: The bill got 22 Democratic cosponsors but no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor vote; it sat in five House committees until the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created a new path for any state (or group of states) to apply for a federal waiver and replace federal health programs in that state with a single, publicly administered state plan. The state would pool the money Washington would otherwise have spent there — Medicare, Medicaid, CHIP, federal employee coverage, TRICARE, and premium tax credits — and use it to cover residents, with a requirement to reach 95% coverage within five years. It was an option states could take up or leave, not a mandate.
analysis.who_benefits: Residents of states that chose to adopt it. Any state could apply to consolidate federal health funds into one state-run plan covering all residents, with benefits and cost-sharing protections at least as good as the federal programs being replaced. The uninsured and people paying high premiums or out-of-pocket costs in an adopting state would have the most to gain. American Indians and Alaska Natives enrolling through a state plan would have all costs paid by the federal government.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Residents of states that opt in

how_it_helps.text: A state could waive the main requirements of the ACA and related laws and replace federal health programs with one comprehensive, publicly administered state plan covering all residents [S2].

The state would receive the full amount the federal government would otherwise have spent in that state on Medicare, Medicaid, CHIP, federal employee coverage, TRICARE, and premium tax credits, adjusted for inflation and caseload growth, plus any administrative savings [S3].

Coverage and cost-sharing must be at least as comprehensive and affordable as what residents would have gotten from the federal programs being replaced, and the state must reach 95% coverage of residents within five years or risk losing the waiver [S2].

An independent panel including patient advocates, nurses, and primary care and rural providers would review each state application, and every approved program would be independently reviewed every five years [S2].

American Indians and Alaska Natives who enroll through a state program would have all costs paid by the federal government, with no premiums or cost sharing, and providers could not be paid less than comparable rates [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal requirement is budget-neutral, so the federal government keeps spending roughly what it would have anyway. The cost falls on the health insurance industry in an adopting state, which loses the premium revenue and gatekeeping role of the private and employer-based coverage the state plan replaces. If a state's health costs grew faster than the federal inflation adjustment, the state's own taxpayers would have to cover the gap. States also retain flexibility to contract with private entities to administer the plan.
analysis.who_pays_short: Private health insurers in adopting states

drawbacks.text: Funding is capped at what the federal programs would have spent in the state, adjusted for health-cost inflation; a state whose costs rose faster would have to make up the difference from its own budget [S3].

The bill requires a 10-year federal budget-neutral plan, so a state cannot use it to bring in new federal money; scaling up coverage has to be financed from pooled existing funds or state revenue [S3].

States may contract with private entities to administer the plan and may not preclude purchase of extra coverage, so a state could still route parts of the system through private intermediaries and layer supplemental private insurance on top [S3].

A state that misses the 95% coverage target gets only a 12-month grace period before the waiver can be terminated, which could leave a partially built state program scrambling to return to the federal programs [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For residents of a state that chose to opt in, the upside is large — a single publicly accountable plan covering everyone, financed by pooling money already being spent. The design acknowledges the risks with a real enforcement mechanism: coverage targets, five-year independent reviews, and possible termination. The main structural weaknesses are that the funding formula is rigid (no new federal money, inflation-adjusted only) and that administration could still be partly outsourced to private contractors.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to five House committees and its Health Subcommittee on day one, and no committee ever took it up, so it never reached a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Ro Khanna introduced the bill on November 8, 2019, with 15 initial cosponsors including Reps. Jayapal, Ocasio-Cortez, Omar, and Pressley [S1].

It was referred that day to five committees — Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Oversight and Reform, Armed Services, and Education and Labor — and three days later to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee [S5].
It drew 22 cosponsors, all Democrats, out of 231 House Democrats [S4].
The action history shows no hearings, no markups, no committee votes, and no floor action for the rest of the 116th Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private health insurers and the employer-based benefits system, which kept the existing coverage structure intact because no state ever got the option to replace it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private health insurers and the status quo

for.name: Ro Khanna
for.what_they_did: Introduced the State-Based Universal Health Care Act and recruited cosponsors.

for.name: 22 of 231 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican cosponsored it.

against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill during the two-year Congress, leaving it without a path to the floor.

against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor; no floor vote occurred at any point in the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 22 cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican signed on; the bill came from the progressive wing of the House Democratic caucus, and the Democratic majority's committees declined to move it.

industries.note: In any state that adopted a waiver, the state plan would replace most private coverage roles — marketplace plans, Medicaid managed care, and Medicare Advantage — with a publicly administered program, though states could still contract with private administrators and residents could buy supplemental coverage. The industry's interest in this bill was keeping the status quo in place, which is what happened.
Waiver states could fold federal employee coverage, TRICARE, and employer tax credits into the state plan, shrinking the employer-sponsored and benefits-administration business in those states.

industries.industry: Tribal and Indian Health Service providers
industries.note: The federal government would pay all costs for American Indians and Alaska Natives enrolling in a state plan, with no cost sharing and payment protections for Indian health care providers.
